add_eyes.name: Harry S. Truman
add_eyes.role: 34-year-old captain commanding Battery D, 129th Field Artillery, 35th Division, AEF; a Missouri farmer and National Guardsman
add_eyes.where: Battery D's firing positions on the old Verdun battlefields, east of Verdun (approximate)
add_eyes.vantage_label: artillery battery commander firing up to the last morning
add_eyes.authenticity: Original letters to Bess Wallace are in the Truman Papers at the Harry S. Truman Library; digitised and transcribed on Missouri Over There. Letters, not a diary; published in 'Dear Bess' (ed. Robert H. Ferrell, 1983).
add_eyes.bio: Truman reenlisted at 33 and took command of a rowdy Irish-Catholic Kansas City battery in July 1918, leading it through the Meuse-Argonne. His letters to his future wife are businesslike, boastful about rounds fired, and contemptuous of the enemy. Thirty years later, as President, he would end another world war.

sources.title: Missouri Over There: Truman letter to Bess Wallace, 11 November 1918
Missouri Over There: Truman letter to Bess Wallace, 1 November 1918
National Park Service: Captain Harry Truman

add_eyes.name: Harry Frieman
add_eyes.role: Private, U.S. infantry (unit not stated in the source consulted)
add_eyes.where: In the line somewhere in France on 11 November 1918 (exact place not given in the source; coordinates are a rough placeholder on the AEF front)
add_eyes.vantage_label: infantry private at the front when the guns stopped
add_eyes.authenticity: Original pocket diary held by the Library of Congress Veterans History Project (collection AFC 2001/001/23600), digitised page by page; the 11 November 1918 page is featured on the Library's Teaching with the Library blog. Unit and service details could not be confirmed here.
add_eyes.bio: An ordinary doughboy whose diary survives only because a family gave it to the Veterans History Project. His Armistice entry is the opposite of a victory parade: relief at having survived a situation that was about to go very badly.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Teaching with the Library: different responses to the Armistice (Frieman diary page)

add_eyes.name: Harvey Cushing
add_eyes.role: American neurosurgeon, aged 46–49; head of a Harvard unit at the American Ambulance, Neuilly (1915), then director of U.S. Base Hospital No. 5 attached to the BEF (1917–18)
add_eyes.side: United States (with British and French forces)
add_eyes.where: Neuilly (Paris) in 1915; Base Hospital No. 5 near Boulogne / Camiers and casualty clearing stations in Flanders, 1917–18
add_eyes.vantage_label: surgeon behind the lines, operating on head wounds
add_eyes.authenticity: Cushing kept a voluminous war journal (manuscript volumes at Yale). He cut and edited it into 'From a Surgeon's Journal, 1915–1918' (Little, Brown, 1936); his publisher reported sentences were selected rather than rewritten, but the printed text is a 1930s selection.
add_eyes.bio: The founder of modern neurosurgery spent much of the war at British casualty clearing stations, pioneering techniques for brain wounds (including pulling shell fragments out with a magnet). His journal records the surgeon's eye on the war, and the deaths of friends: his mentor William Osler lost his son Revere, mortally wounded in Flanders in August 1917, and Cushing buried the poet John McCrae in 1918.

sources.title: Yale Library online exhibit: Peter Bent Brigham Hospital & War Service
Cushing and his editor (historyofscience.com PDF, with journal extracts)
JAMA 1936 review of From a Surgeon's Journal

add_eyes.name: Florence Farmborough
add_eyes.role: English governess and tutor in Moscow who qualified as a Red Cross nurse in 1914 and served with a Russian front-line field surgical unit, aged 27–30
add_eyes.where: Galician front from Gorlice (spring 1915), then the Great Retreat through Galicia and Poland toward Minsk; later the Brusilov advance and the Romanian front
add_eyes.vantage_label: field nurse with the retreating Russian army
add_eyes.authenticity: She kept a diary of about 400,000 words at the front and took photographs with a plate camera, developing them in camp. A cut selection was published as 'Nurse at the Russian Front: A Diary 1914–18' (Constable, 1974; US title 'With the Armies of the Tsar'). Her photographs are at the Imperial War Museum. Dates below are as given by a secondary quotation site; she often gives Old Style alongside New Style.
add_eyes.bio: Farmborough is the rare Western eye inside the Tsar's army: an Englishwoman who spoke Russian and dressed wounds in tents while the front collapsed around her. Her 1915 diary records the scorched-earth retreat, Cossacks burning villages, and the new word 'refugee', from the ranks of the Russian army itself rather than from the palace.

sources.title: IWM: object from Florence Farmborough's service

add_eyes.name: Edward Percy Cox
add_eyes.role: Captain (later Major), Wellington Infantry Battalion, NZEF, service number 10/659
add_eyes.where: Anzac Cove and Walker's Ridge, Gallipoli
add_eyes.vantage_label: New Zealand company officer at the landing
add_eyes.authenticity: Original diary held by Te Papa Tongarewa (Museum of New Zealand); Cox kept it contrary to army regulations. Transcribed online by the NZ Electronic Text Collection (Victoria University of Wellington) as 'Gallipoli Diary', and read in episodes by RNZ. It runs from October 1914 to 5 August 1915; he was wounded on 8 August at Chunuk Bair.
add_eyes.bio: Cox sailed with the main body in October 1914, trained in Egypt, and landed at Anzac on the evening of 25 April 1915. His diary gives the New Zealand view of the first weeks: the waiting off Lemnos, the beach under fire, the losses on Walker's Ridge. It stops on the eve of the August offensive in which he was wounded.

sources.title: NZETC: Cox, Gallipoli Diary — Sunday 25 April 1915
NZETC: Cox, Gallipoli Diary — Thursday 29 April 1915, Walker's Ridge
DigitalNZ / Te Papa: diary of Major E. P. Cox

add_entries.place: Transport Itonus, Lemnos to Anzac Cove
add_entries.headline: Hearing the guns, then landing at Anzac before midnight
add_entries.digest: The Itonus leaves Lemnos at six in a calm sea and the men are cheerful; gunfire from the Dardanelles is already audible forty miles off. A church service at nine is made solemn by the bombardment. By four in the afternoon the ship is off Kaba Tepe, and from six the New Zealanders go ashore by destroyer. Cox writes up what he has heard of the Australian dawn landing and its heavy losses, then lands himself shortly before midnight to dig in near corps headquarters.
add_entries.source_note: Cox, Gallipoli Diary, pp. 40–41, entry 'Sunday Apr 25/15 Lemnos' (NZETC transcription).

add_entries.headline: Walker's Ridge: two hundred men gone since Sunday
add_entries.digest: Cox's men keep deepening their trenches under fierce, intermittent rifle fire; he does not expect a Turkish assault but says they are ready. The regiment has lost about seven officers and two hundred men since the landing, the Taranaki company forty-five of them, mostly on the Tuesday. There are no howitzers and no room for field guns, heavy shells from the Goeben or the forts fall near the ships, and the weather, he notes, is perfect.
add_entries.source_note: Cox, Gallipoli Diary, entry 'Thursday 29/4/15 Walker's Ridge' (NZETC transcription).

add_entries.headline: New Zealand will now see the other side of war
add_entries.digest: After the battalion is pulled back to the beach, Cox reflects on what the first fortnight has cost. People at home, he writes, will now understand for the first time the horrors of war, not just its glory.
add_entries.source_note: Te Papa diary of E. P. Cox, 6 May 1915 entry, as described on DigitalNZ record 47727; RNZ 'The Soldier's Diary' part 21.

add_entries.place: On the move with the Russian retreat, Galicia
add_entries.headline: 'Refugee' becomes a word of every day
add_entries.digest: Travelling across plain and woodland with her unit, Farmborough sees displaced families everywhere. She hears that Cossacks have orders to drive villagers out so they cannot spy for the enemy, and sees homesteads burned and crops destroyed. Refugee, she notes, has become part of her daily vocabulary, and for weeks her unit's work is bound up with them.
add_entries.source_note: Nurse at the Russian Front (1974), as excerpted on WWI Today (id 428); date as given there, calendar style not stated.

add_entries.headline: A man falls under a gun carriage and is left
add_entries.digest: In the chaos of the retreat a man falls under a gun carriage and the column simply keeps moving. Enemy aircraft circle overhead and shells land just behind her unit.
add_entries.source_note: Nurse at the Russian Front (1974), as excerpted on WWI Today (id 427); calendar style not stated.

add_entries.date_display: Monday 2 August 1915 (night of 1 August N.S. / 19 July O.S.)
add_entries.headline: Cossacks burn the village they are retreating through
add_entries.digest: Woken by shouts that the village is on fire, Farmborough finds Rymachi in ruins by morning. A peasant woman says she watched Cossacks, 'our own Russians', set a thatched roof alight, and asks what the poor can do when their own people turn on them. The soldiers blame German spies; the villagers quietly blame the Cossacks. It is scorched earth, seen from inside the army doing it.
add_entries.source_note: Nurse at the Russian Front (1974), as excerpted on WWI Today (id 466), with O.S./N.S. dates given.

add_entries.headline: The Great Retreat is over
add_entries.digest: As her party leaves Minsk to rejoin their division, Russian anti-aircraft guns fire at an enemy plane circling the town. They are glad to put Minsk behind them; after months of falling back, the retreat has ended and she feels like a new person.
add_entries.source_note: Nurse at the Russian Front (1974), as excerpted on WWI Today (id 530).

add_entries.headline: Advancing this time, through flowering land
add_entries.digest: A year after the retreat, the Russians are moving forward in the Brusilov offensive. Farmborough contrasts the defeats of 1915 with the successes of the Russian and Allied armies now, and feels the relief, but notes the wreckage the advancing troops leave in fields still in flower.
add_entries.source_note: Nurse at the Russian Front (1974), as excerpted on WWI Today (id 835).

add_entries.headline: A magnet fails; a wire nail pulls the steel out
add_entries.digest: After several failed attempts with a magnet to draw a steel fragment from a soldier's brain, Cushing's team tries again with a wire nail, and this time the rough little fragment comes out clinging to its tip. It is a small technical triumph that he records with obvious delight, the surgeon's war in miniature.
add_entries.source_note: From a Surgeon's Journal (1936), Neuilly entry of 29 April 1915, as quoted in 'Cushing and his editor' (historyofscience.com).

add_entries.headline: John McCrae dies of pneumonia in a hospital bed
add_entries.digest: Cushing records the death of the Canadian physician-poet John McCrae, author of 'In Flanders Fields', from pneumonia and meningitis at Boulogne. He thinks of him as a soldier through and through, and reflects how much McCrae would have hated dying in bed rather than in the field. The next day he describes the burial at Wimereux with military honours.
add_entries.source_note: From a Surgeon's Journal (1936), entries of 28 and 29 January 1918, as quoted in 'Cushing and his editor' (historyofscience.com).

add_entries.headline: 1,800 shells in five hours, and a German predicts peace
add_entries.digest: Truman tells Bess he has just put eighteen hundred shells over on the Germans in five hours. A German airman who has come down behind the battery shouts that the war is finished and will end within ten days; Truman's men strip the wreck for souvenirs, and he doubts anyone really knows when it will end.
add_entries.source_note: Truman to Bess Wallace, 1 November 1918 (Truman Papers; Missouri Over There transcription). A letter, not a diary.

add_entries.place: Brandenburg Gate to the Reichstag, Berlin
add_entries.headline: Soldiers tear off their cockades; she thinks of Peter
add_entries.digest: Kollwitz walks with the crowd from the Brandenburg Gate to the Reichstag, where Scheidemann proclaims the Republic from a window. Soldiers, sailors and a young officer address the crowd under red flags, and soldiers rip the imperial cockades from their caps. That morning workers had marched with placards asking soldiers not to shoot. Watching the young men, she thinks of her dead son.
add_entries.source_note: Kollwitz diary, 9 November 1918, German History in Documents and Images (GHDI), 'Käthe Kollwitz on the Revolution 1918–19'.

add_entries.place: Bismarck monument by the Reichstag, Berlin
add_entries.headline: A pacifist rally scattered three times by gunfire
add_entries.digest: At a pacifist rally near the Reichstag the speeches are broken off three times by shooting and once by cannon fire; each time the crowd scatters and drifts back. She records rumours that royalist officers have hidden machine guns. The entry also contains a remark generalising about revolutionary leaders being Jewish, a prejudice of its moment that the source flags.

add_entries.headline: The last shot of the world war has been fired
add_entries.digest: Kollwitz welcomes the agreement between the two socialist parties and reads the published armistice terms, hoping the real peace will be gentler. Her husband Karl's faith in the revolution steadies her. Rumours about the Kaiser's flight and Hindenburg mingle with the Vorwärts headline announcing that the last shot of the war has been fired, and she stops on that line to think.

add_entries.place: Water meadows below Cuddesdon, Oxfordshire; evening in London
add_entries.headline: Flags, bells and mob patriotism: a loathsome ending
add_entries.digest: In the morning Sassoon walks by the river in grey weather while church bells ring and villagers hang out flags; he writes that the news is impossible to take in. He reaches London at about half past six to find crowds jamming the streets and Tube, which he reads as mob patriotism, and argues over dinner in Cheyne Walk with fellow guests about the celebrations. He sums up the day as a loathsome end to a loathsome four-year tragedy.
add_entries.source_note: Sassoon journal, 11 November 1918, transcribed on the Cambridge University Library Special Collections blog ('Sassoon's journal entry for Armistice Day').

add_entries.place: Battery D, 129th Field Artillery, near Verdun
add_entries.headline: Firing to the last half hour
add_entries.digest: On YMCA paper Truman writes that official word has just come that hostilities will cease at eleven, with the German deadline for acceptance thirty minutes away. A neighbouring 155mm battery has been firing almost as fast as a 75 for two hours; he himself fired 164 rounds that morning, bringing the battery past ten thousand rounds. He wishes Germany could be made to work for France and Belgium for fifty years.
add_entries.source_note: Truman to Bess Wallace, 11 November 1918 (Missouri Over There transcription); NPS notes the 129th fired its last shots fifteen minutes before the Armistice.

add_entries.headline: A few more hours and few would be left
add_entries.digest: After the cease-fire at eleven, Frieman's unit discovers that German troops had all but surrounded it. He writes that if the war had gone on a few hours longer there would not have been many of them left to tell the story. Relief, not jubilation, is the note of the page.
add_entries.source_note: Frieman diary, 11 November 1918, Library of Congress Veterans History Project (AFC 2001/001/23600, p. 56), as reproduced on the LOC Teaching with the Library blog.

add_convergences.label: Armistice Day, 11 November 1918
add_convergences.note: Truman is still firing at 10.30 and boasting of his ten-thousandth round; Frieman, somewhere in the American line, realises his unit was nearly surrounded and calls it a narrow escape. In Berlin Kessler gives the day one bare line and Kollwitz lingers on a newspaper headline about the last shot. Sassoon, safe in Oxfordshire, hears the bells and calls the London crowds mob patriotism. Victory, relief, defeat and disgust on one Monday.

add_convergences.label: The Anzac landing, 25 April 1915
add_convergences.note: Cox hears the bombardment from forty miles out and lands before midnight to dig in; in Jerusalem, Turjman spends the same day at an expensive dinner, with the landing far away. The same date is the founding day of a nation's memory for one and an ordinary evening for the other.

add_ties.note: Both landed at Anzac with the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps; Cox's battalion held Walker's Ridge on the beachhead Bean was describing day by day.
Cox fought from the Anzac beachhead in April–August 1915; Fasih's battalion held Ottoman trenches facing the same perimeter that autumn.
Both American soldiers wrote on 11 November 1918 from the AEF line in France, one an artillery captain still firing, the other an infantry private counting himself lucky.
Both walked Berlin's streets on 9–11 November 1918 and both recorded the shooting near the Reichstag; neither diary mentions the other.

fix.note: Kessler walks through the Berlin revolution and gives the Armistice a single line; Kollwitz, also in Berlin, marches to the Reichstag on the 9th, is scattered by gunfire at a pacifist rally on the 10th, and on the 11th fixes on the headline that the last shot has been fired. For the Armistice itself seen from the Allied side, see the separate 11 November convergence.
